article_lead.description: conditional count variation smaller than a fitted reference model predicts, which changes uncertainty estimates

new_bank_questions.title: A binomial count below Poisson variance
new_bank_questions.body: A count is binomial with five trials and success probability 0.4. Find its mean, variance and variance-to-mean ratio. Compare its variance with a Poisson count having the same mean.
new_bank_questions.answer: The mean is 5(0.4)=2 and the variance is 5(0.4)(0.6)=1.2. Its variance-to-mean ratio is 1.2/2=0.6. A Poisson count with mean 2 has variance 2, so this binomial mechanism is underdispersed relative to that Poisson reference.

new_bank_questions.title: Conditional spread versus pooled spread
new_bank_questions.body: Five units in group A each have count 1; five in group B each have count 5. Compute the pooled sample mean and variance, then describe the within-group variance. Why can a pooled mean–variance comparison misdiagnose dispersion?
new_bank_questions.answer: The pooled mean is 3 and the pooled sample variance is 40/9≈4.444, greater than the pooled mean. Within each group the sample variance is zero. The group indicator explains the mean shift; dispersion should be assessed conditional on fitted group means rather than from the pooled counts.
